query: Why is elevated-temperature mechanical testing important for aerospace structural alloys, and what does it reveal that room-temperature testing does not? Cover, with citations and DOIs: (1) Where aerospace structures get hot: aerodynamic heating of supersonic and hypersonic skins (Concorde at Mach 2 cruise, the NASA High-Speed Research / HSCT program, missiles and hypersonic vehicles), engine nacelles, pylons, thrust reversers and bleed-air ducts, auxiliary power units, compressor wheels and impellers, heat exchangers, structures near rocket engines and thermal-protection-system substructure, and fire exposure. (2) What changes with temperature and with time at temperature: loss of yield and tensile strength, elongation and modulus at temperature; property loss after thermal exposure (overaging, precipitate coarsening) measured back at room temperature; creep, stress rupture and stress relaxation; low-cycle and thermomechanical fatigue and creep-fatigue interaction; fatigue-crack growth and fracture toughness at temperature; oxidation; dynamic strain aging; and how long-time behavior is extrapolated (Larson-Miller, Wilshire, Monkman-Grant). (3) How design allowables handle temperature: MMPDS 'effect of temperature' and 'effect of exposure time' curves (for example 0.5 h to 10,000 h), and how this differs for aluminum, titanium, steels and nickel superalloys. (4) Test standards and practice: ASTM E21 (elevated-temperature tension), ISO 6892-2, ASTM E139 and ISO 204 (creep and stress rupture), ASTM E328 (stress relaxation), ASTM E606 (strain-controlled fatigue), ASTM E2368 (thermomechanical fatigue), ASTM E2714 (creep-fatigue), ASTM E1457 (creep-crack growth); heating methods, temperature-uniformity and soak-time requirements, and high-temperature extensometry. (5) Failures, anomalies or design changes traced to missing or inadequate elevated-temperature property data. Context: the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab designs aluminum alloys for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with AI and CALPHAD, including critical-mineral-lean compositions (less Sc, Li, Ce), makes its own powder by ultrasonic atomization, and tests in a ladder of single tracks, density cubes and room-temperature tensile bars. It is deciding which elevated-temperature, non-tensile and rate-dependent mechanical tests to add. Prefer primary sources, NASA, NIST and AFRL technical reports, MMPDS and standards; give DOIs or report numbers; give numbers with temperatures, exposure times, strain rates and units; and say which claims are strongly vs. weakly supported.
task_summary: Elevated Temperature Mechanical Testing Needs For Aerospace Alloys Covering Locations Mechanisms Standards And Design Allowables

info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Use the tools to answer the question: Why is elevated-temperature mechanical testing important for aerospace structural alloys, and what does it reveal that room-temperature testing does not? Cover, with citations and DOIs: (1) Where aerospace structures get hot: aerodynamic heating of supersonic and hypersonic skins (Concorde at Mach 2 cruise, the NASA High-Speed Research / HSCT program, missiles and hypersonic vehicles), engine nacelles, pylons, thrust reversers and bleed-air ducts, auxiliary power units, compressor wheels and impellers, heat exchangers, structures near rocket engines and thermal-protection-system substructure, and fire exposure. Abstract:
Considering the influence of thermal stress and material property variations, this study employs the Navier–Stokes equations and Fourier heat conduction law to establish a semi-implicit time-domain numerical analysis method for hypersonic aerothermal-structural coupling. Study the temporal variation pattern of different regions of the composite material wing under aerodynamic heating. Using the obtained transient temperature field of the wing, the thermal modal of the wing at different time points is calculated using the finite element method. Additionally, it conducts an analysis and discussion on the factors influencing the thermal modal. Composites can be effectively utilized as thermal protection materials for aircraft. During the aerodynamic heating process, the leading edge temperature reaches thermal equilibrium first, followed by the trailing edge, and the belly plate experiences a slower thermal response. Temperature rise significantly affects higher-order modes, with the change in material properties during the early stages of heating being the dominant factor. This leads to a faster decrease in natural frequency. As heat conduction progresses, the influencing factors of thermal stresses gradually increase, and the natural frequency decreases slowly or even rises.

Abstract:
The results of untiring efforts by the research community over the past few decades have led to the successful development and processing of a number of advanced titanium alloys with widely varying properties that can cater to niche applications. Advanced titanium alloys on one hand challenge structural steels with their higher specific strength coupled with their low temperature capability down to 4 K and pose serious threat on the other hand to superalloys for long-term applications up to 773 K. An improved understanding of the processing-microstructure-mechanical property correlation led to the realization of large scale as well as performance critical titanium alloy products in space arena. Recent advances in additive manufacturing, wherein the desired components are directly 3D printed from pre-alloyed powders/wires have given a definite advantage for cost-prohibitive titanium alloys. This review article discusses challenges in the processing, mechanical properties and microstructure evolution of various grades of titanium alloys. It also provides useful information for researchers working on titanium alloys with a glimpse in to the recent advances in Ti alloys and transformation of scientific knowledge to technological advancements in products for space applications.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The aircraft is subjected to high-temperature and high-pressure conditions during flight, which renders it susceptible to the occurrence of creep phenomenon. Several academics have conducted extensive research on this issue. This research paper provides a comprehensive overview of the existing literature on creep phenomena in aircraft engines. First, several classical creep calculation models are enumerated and categorized as creep life calculation, creep-fatigue life calculation, and creep deformation calculation. Studies on creep phenomena are conducted in various components of aircraft engines, such as the engine’s turbine blades, turbine disks, and combustion chambers. The creep behavior of turbine blades in aircraft engines has been extensively researched. Furthermore, the protective measures aimed at mitigating creep are presented. Materials with high creep resistance can be used, and alternative fuels could be implemented. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the advantages of creep in aircraft, presented in a favorable perspective. Finally, the prospective future research direction is discussed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Creep is defined as the permanent deformation of materials under the effect of sustained stress and elevated temperature for long periods of time, which can essentially lead to fracture. Due to very time-consuming and expensive testing requirements, existing experimental creep data are often analyzed using derived engineering parameters and models to predict and find the correlations between creep life (time to rupture), temperature and stress. The objective of this study was to analyze and compare different numerical algorithms by using the Larson–Miller parameter (LMP) extrapolation model. Calculations were performed using the classical LMP equation where different values of parameter C were selected, as well as using a modified LMP equation in which parameter C was stress dependent C(σ). The impact of two different approaches of extrapolation and correlation functions (linear and polynomial) applied to fit the LMP model was also investigated. A detailed analysis was performed to choose the best extrapolation fit function and error tolerance. The numerical algorithm implemented was validated through creep rupture testing performed on 10CrMo9–10 steel at 600 °C (873 K) and 80 MPa. Creep model behavior analysis proved that different values of C can significantly change the estimated time to rupture. An excellent response of the LMP model was obtained by considering polynomial dependency when parameter C was assumed to be 18, especially for the temperature range from 773 to 873 K. Promising results were also achieved when parameter C was taken as stress-dependent, but only for linear fitting, which requires further analysis. However, at validation stage it turned out that only the linear extrapolation function and C taken as a constant value provided adequate time-to-rupture prediction. In the case of C = 18, estimated time was slightly overestimated (~8%) and for C = 20 it was underestimated by 27%. In all other cases error largely exceeded 50%.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This paper presents the results of a detailed experimental study into the mechanical properties of ASTM A992 structural steel at elevated temperatures. Critical testing issues, including temperature measurement, temperature control, and extensometer use along with the testing equipment and procedures are briefly explained. Tensile steady-state temperature tests are conducted on samples of ASTM A992 steel at temperatures up to 1000 Â°C. Full stress-strain curves, representing steel coupons tested to fracture at elevated temperatures, are generated. Important mechanical properties such as yield stress, tensile strength, proportional limit, elastic modulus and elongation are obtained from the stress-strain curves. Results are compared with elevated-temperature properties specified by Eurocode 3 and by the AISC Specification. When defined as the stress at 2% total strain, the measured yield stress values agree reasonably well with the corresponding values from Eurocode 3 and the AISC Specification. However, for more conventional definitions of yield stress, such as the 0.2% offset yield stress, the agreement is poor. It is observed that the yield stress of steel at elevated temperatures up to about 600 Â°C is highly dependent on the manner in which yield stress is defined. The effects of displacement loading rates on steel strength and static yielding behavior are also investigated. It is shown that the displacement rate has a large impact on the steel strength at elevated temperatures, especially at temperatures higher than 600 Â°C. Further work is needed to fully characterize the time-dependent effects on the elevated-temperature stress-strain response of structural steel. Additionally, this paper presents results of Charpy V-Notch (CVN) tests on ASTM A992 steel at elevated temperatures.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This study concerns the quasi-static and time-dependent mechanical behavior obtained via the miniaturized electro-thermal mechanical testing (ETMT) approach for single crystal (SX) and conventional cast Mar-M-247 superalloy. The experimental outcome was benchmarked against standardized testing procedures. It is found that tensile yielding behavior can be captured accurately by the ETMT approach up to 1100 $$^{\circ }$$ ∘ C, provided the appropriate type of thermocouple (T/C) is chosen. Furthermore, creep rupture behavior is underestimated by the miniaturized set-up. High repeatability of the rupture time was obtained for the SX case, whereas a significant scatter was observed for the conventional cast case. The discrepancies are assessed in detail; discussion centers around analytical and practical considerations, such as temperature uncertainty due to parasitic voltage and the choice of T/C, microstructural change as a result of the Joule heating, representative gauge volume, and strain rate non-linearity. Consequently, the applicability and limits of the miniaturized approach are examined critically, and improvements were suggested where appropriate.

Abstract:

 Nickel-based superalloys operate primarily in high-temperature environments where their unique microstructure provides operational capability far in excess of many other engineering materials. As such these materials often operate in applications where thermal cycles occur alongside mechanical fatigue, giving rise to the phenomenon of thermo-mechanical fatigue (TMF). The field of study of TMF has historically been limited due to the need for improved experimental methods to replicate in-service cycles appropriately and provide usable data for component lifing. With the development of international test standards the field has developed rapidly over the past two decades and this paper seeks to review the recent work in the field in the areas of both single crystal and polycrystalline materials to provide a state of the art summary of the current position of the field related to durability and failure mechanisms.

Abstract:
Abstract Plastic deformation processes are among the most demanding processes in manufacturing because they lead to different microstructure features in the materials produced. Various dislocation patterns can be induced by plastic strain under different conditions. A serrated yielding/jerky flow in some dilute alloys, such as aluminium-magnesium alloys during plastic deformation, is a well-known phenomenon under certain regimes of strain rate and temperature, as reported in a significant number of works. The serrated features in these materials reflect the so-called Portevin-Le Chatelier effects. These undesirable effects are due to the interaction between solute atoms and mobile dislocation during the plastic deformation, which is known as dynamic strain ageing. There are a significant number of theoretical and numerical investigations that have focused on describing the serrated behaviours of these materials during plastic deformation. Hence, the fundamental objective of this paper is to provide a general review of different constitutive modelling in regards this feature. The typical material models and new constitutive models describing this feature are presented. In addition, applications of the models are provided along with their respective advantages and disadvantages.

Abstract:
Serrated flow effects are visible on a metal surface even after coating. Thus, they are undesirable to manufacturers and product users. To meet the expectations of the industry, research on the conditions for serrated flow occurrence in 5019 aluminum alloy was carried out and the results were collected in the current paper. Thus, the influence of the alloy initial microstructure due to different tempers as well as plastic deformation conditions, i.e., strain rate and temperature, on the alloy stress–strain behavior was determined. Two tempers were considered: the as-fabricated F-temper and the W-temper (i.e., quenched in water after annealing at 500 °C). The synergic influence of these tempers and their tensile test conditions on the serration behavior of the stress–strain curves, i.e., the stress drop and reloading time, were also determined and categorized. Structural and X-ray diffraction studies rationalized the stress–strain characteristics according to dynamic strain aging models with positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy providing insight into the role of lattice defects (i.e., dislocations and vacancies). The map of the serrated flow domain allowed us to obtain the activation energy of the onset of the Portevin–Le Chatelier effect equal to 56 kJ/mol. It is close to the activation energy for the pipe diffusion mechanism, obtained by applying the model formulated originally for Type B stress serration.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Due to their excellent corrosion resistance, light weight, hardenability, and high recyclability, aluminum alloys have become a staple in the automotive industry, particularly in the manufacturing of car bodies. However, the Portevin–Le Chatelier (PLC) effect, which manifests in certain aluminum alloys during plastic deformation, poses significant challenges. This phenomenon can lead to undesirable visual and structural defects, thereby limiting the broader application of these alloys in the automotive sector. Understanding the PLC effect is crucial for enhancing the usability of aluminum alloys in vehicle production. This paper deals with the PLC phenomenon, exploring the various parameters that influence its occurrence during plastic processing. By investigating these factors, the aim is to provide a better insight on this phenomenon.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The Wilshire creep equations were introduced around fifteen years ago. Their aim was to address the non-physical extrapolation of power-law models, especially to high stresses, and the unrealistic values for activation energy and stress exponent that often arise from simple fits to data. In application they have met with some success, also with some difficulties which have largely been addressed empirically. No detailed mathematical analysis of the model seems to have been performed. This paper considers the fundamental characteristics of the Wilshire equations, as originally given, commencing with their internal consistency. It is found that the strain-time equation is incompatible with those for minimum creep-rate and rupture life. A consistent rate equation is derived, enabling the model to address the creep process rather than merely its results. Predictions made using the original and developed models are compared with actual materials behaviour; this reveals aspects of the approach which require reconsideration. The upper limit imposed by the ultimate tensile strength, and departures from a simple power law emerge as the key characteristics to be preserved and considered further.

Abstract:
Creep tests were carried out on notched plate specimens of nickel-based superalloy GH4169 with different stress concentration coefficients. It was found that the duration of the first stage of the creep curve increases with the increase of stress concentration coefficient, while the fracture ductility decreases with the increase of stress concentration coefficient. To predict the life of notched plate specimens, four constitutive models were used to analyze the stress and strain of the notches. It was found that the average Von Mises equivalent stress (AVES) on the minimum notch section first decreases and then increases with the creep time, resulting in a minimum value. The minimum average Von Mises equivalent stress (MAVES) is considered as the characteristic stress of notched specimens in this paper. The creep life equation is fitted according to the results of creep tests of smooth specimens, and then the predicted life of notched specimens is obtained by substituting the minimum average Von Mises equivalent stress of notched specimens into the creep equation. The prediction results of the four constitutive models are within 2 times the dispersion band, and the three-stage model is within the 1.5 times dispersion band.

Abstract:
The present study is dedicated to the evaluation of the mechanical properties of an additively manufactured (AM) aluminum alloy and their dependence on temperature and build orientation. Tensile test samples were produced from a standard AlSi10Mg alloy by means of the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) or Laser Beam Melting (LBM) process at polar angles of 0°, 45° and 90°. Prior to testing, samples were stress-relieved on the build platform for 2 h at 350 °C. Tensile tests were performed at four temperature levels (room temperature (RT), 125, 250 and 450 °C). Results are compared to previously published data on AM materials with and without comparable heat treatment. To foster a deeper understanding of the obtained results, fracture surfaces were analyzed, and metallographic sections were prepared for microstructural evaluation and for additional hardness measurements. The study confirms the expected significant reduction of strength at elevated temperatures and specifically above 250 °C: Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) was found to be 280.2 MPa at RT, 162.8 MPa at 250 °C and 34.4 MPa at 450 °C for a polar angle of 0°. In parallel, elongation at failure increased from 6.4% via 15.6% to 26.5%. The influence of building orientation is clearly dominated by the temperature effect, with UTS values at RT for polar angles of 0° (vertical), 45° and 90° (horizontal) reaching 280.2, 272.0 and 265.9 MPa, respectively, which corresponds to a 5.1% deviation. The comparatively low room temperature strength of roughly 280 MPa is associated with stress relieving and agrees well with data from the literature. However, the complete breakdown of the cellular microstructure reported in other studies for treatments at similar or slightly lower temperatures is not fully confirmed by the metallographic investigations. The data provide a basis for the prediction of AM component response under the thermal and mechanical loads associated with high-pressure die casting (HPDC) and thus facilitate optimizing HPDC-based compound casting processes involving AM inserts.

Abstract:
Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy processed via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is poised for significant application in aerospace, where its high-temperature capabilities are paramount for the safety and longevity of engineered structures. This study offers a systematic examination of the alloy’s high-temperature tensile properties in relation to its microstructure and precipitate phases, utilizing experimental approaches. The LPBF-processed Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy features a bimodal microstructure, with columnar grains in the melt pool’s interior and equiaxed grains along its boundary, conferring exceptional properties. The application of well-calibrated processing parameters has yielded an alloy with an impressive relative density of 99.8%, nearly fully dense. Following a thermal treatment of 350 °C for 4 h, the specimens were subjected to tensile tests at both room and elevated temperatures. The data reveal that the specimens exhibit a tensile strength of 560.6 MPa and an elongation of 11.1% at room temperature. A predictable decline in tensile strength with rising temperature is observed: at 100 °C, 150 °C, 200 °C, and 250 °C; the respective strengths and elongations are 435.1 MPa and 25.8%, 269.4 MPa and 20.1%, 102.8 MPa and 47.9%, 54.0 MPa and 72.2%. These findings underpin the technical rationale for employing LPBF-processed Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy in aerospace applications.

One potential technological advantage of aluminium additive manufacturing, however, has received little attention: the design of alloys for use at T > ∼200°C, or ∼1/2 of the absolute melting temperature of aluminium. Besides offering lightweighting and improved energy efficiency through replacement of ferrous, titanium, and nickel-based alloys at 200–450°C, development of such alloys will reduce economic roadblocks for widespread implementation of aluminium additive manufacturing. Abstract:
Due to its lightweight, high strength, good machinability, and low cost, aluminum alloy has been widely used in fields such as aerospace, automotive, electronics, and construction. Traditional manufacturing processes for aluminum alloys often suffer from low material utilization, complex procedures, and long manufacturing cycles. Therefore, more and more scholars are turning their attention to the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process for aluminum alloys, which has the advantages of high material utilization, good formability for complex structures, and short manufacturing cycles. However, the widespread promotion and application of LPBF aluminum alloys still face challenges. The excellent printable ability, favorable mechanical performance, and low manufacturing cost are the main factors affecting the applicability of the LPBF process for aluminum alloys. This paper reviews the research status of traditional aluminum alloy processing and LPBF aluminum alloy and makes a comparison from various aspects such as microstructures, mechanical properties, application scenarios, and manufacturing costs. At present, the LPBF manufacturing cost for aluminum alloys is 2–120 times higher than that of traditional manufacturing methods, with the discrepancy depending on the complexity of the part. Therefore, it is necessary to promote the further development and application of aluminum alloy 3D printing technology from three aspects: the development of aluminum matrix composite materials reinforced with nanoceramic particles, the development of micro-alloyed aluminum alloy powders specially designed for LPBF, and the development of new technologies and equipment to reduce the manufacturing cost of LPBF aluminum alloy.

Abstract:

 Fiber-reinforced composite (FRC) materials have gained significant traction in various industrial sectors, including aerospace, marine, and energy applications, owing to their outstanding mechanical properties, lightweight nature, high strength, and corrosion resistance. However, ensuring the reliability and durability of these materials under diverse environmental conditions, such as exposure to elevated temperatures, mechanical loads, and chemicals/oxidations, remains a critical challenge. In this study, we provide an in-depth insight into the failure mechanisms of FRC materials under several scenarios expected when in service or during operations, particularly for failure arising from mechanical, thermal, and chemical exposure, which are the main conditions experienced in aircraft, helicopters, drones, wind turbines, and ships. Moreover, we excerpt representative cases that illustrate changes in material properties due to prolonged exposure to an uneven temperature gradient leading to thermal expansion mismatch, matrix softening, and fiber degradation. Also, a critical examination of the stress distribution, damage evolution, and failure criteria of FRC materials due to mechanical loads under the tensile, flexural, impact, and compressive loading conditions through experimental, theoretical, and numerical studies is presented to offer significant contributions to the understanding of failure mechanisms and their consequences for structural design and performance optimization. Thus, chemical and oxidative degradation in FRC materials, including matrix degradation, fiber-matrix interface debonding, and their impact on mechanical properties, has been analyzed. The media include aviation fuels, seawater environments, hydraulic fluids, deicer, and acidic and alkaline solvents. Furthermore, this work includes an overview of numerical and analytical perspectives concerning the tripod (mechanical, thermal, and chemical oxidations). To bring forth a series of models, theories, and assumptions employed by several researchers to recreate real-world applications with very high accuracy to experimental data, a detailed overview of the FRC failure mechanism in various environmental conditions has been reviewed, and gaps that can be explored in future research have been highlighted. Challenges and limitations hindering the accurate screening of composite materials for intended applications have been reported. It is anticipated that scholars, engineers, and researchers engaged in the development and application of the FRC materials in the aerospace, marine, and energy industries will find this review beneficial. It will assist them in comprehending composite failures under different environmental and loading conditions and provide critical insights for advancing the design, manufacturing, durability, and reliability of the FRC-based structures and components in the harsh operating environments.

Abstract:
Over the last two decades, the repair of existing engineering structures using fiber reinforced polymer composites has attracted a great attention by aerospace industry, as it is more economical than replacing new. With an increased use of composite material in aerospace field, it is thus essential to restore the structural integrity by repair of damaged part. Concerns regarding the long term durability of composite repair bonded joints have been a major obstacle for critical component of aerospace structures. This paper reviews the current research on the environmental durability of adhesive bonded repair of composite structures to focus on the durability concerns and suggestion on the research needed in this area. The most important environmental factors (moisture and temperature) are reviewed thoroughly and also combined environmental effect. Finite element methods used to predict the environmental influence on the composite bonded joints are briefly reviewed. Finally, the paper concludes with key findings, opportunities and future research topics in order to develop cost effective, better quality and reliable composite repair bonded joints.

Abstract:
This review article provides an exhaustive survey on experimental investigations regarding the thermal stability assessment of polymers and polymer-based composites intended for applications in the aeronautical and space fields. This review aims to: (1) come up with a systematic and critical overview of the state-of-the-art knowledge and research on the thermal stability of various polymers and composites, such as polyimides, epoxy composites, and carbon-filled composites; (2) identify the key factors, mechanisms, methods, and challenges that affect the thermal stability of polymers and composites, such as the temperature, radiation, oxygen, and degradation; (3) highlight the current and potential applications, benefits, limitations, and opportunities of polymers and composites with high thermal stability, such as thermal control, structural reinforcement, protection, and energy conversion; (4) give a glimpse of future research directions by providing indications for improving the thermal stability of polymers and composites, such as novel materials, hybrid composites, smart materials, and advanced processing methods. In this context, thermal analysis plays a crucial role in the development of polyimide-based materials for the radiation shielding of space solar cells or spacecraft components. The main strategies that have been explored to improve the processability, optical transparency, and radiation resistance of polyimide-based materials without compromising their thermal stability are highlighted. The combination of different types of polyimides, such as linear and hyperbranched, as well as the incorporation of bulky pendant groups, are reported as routes for improving the mechanical behavior and optical transparency while retaining the thermal stability and radiation shielding properties. Furthermore, the thermal stability of polymer/carbon nanocomposites is discussed with particular reference to the role of the filler in radiation monitoring systems and electromagnetic interference shielding in the space environment. Finally, the thermal stability of epoxy-based composites and how it is influenced by the type and content of epoxy resin, curing agent, degree of cross-linking, and the addition of fillers or modifiers are critically reviewed. Some studies have reported that incorporating mesoporous silica micro-filler or microencapsulated phase change materials (MPCM) into epoxy resin can enhance its thermal stability and mechanical properties. The mesoporous silica composite exhibited the highest glass transition temperature and activation energy for thermal degradation among all the epoxy-silica nano/micro-composites. Indeed, an average activation energy value of 148.86 kJ/mol was recorded for the thermal degradation of unfilled epoxy resin. The maximum activation energy range was instead recorded for composites loaded with mesoporous microsilica. The EMC-5p50 sample showed the highest mean value of 217.6 kJ/mol. This remarkable enhancement was ascribed to the polymer invading the silica pores and forging formidable interfacial bonds.

RA Edahl Jr and M Domack. Effect of thermal exposure on the tensile properties of aluminum alloys for elevated temperature service. Unknown journal, 2004.

The excerpt addresses thermal stability of aluminum alloys intended for supersonic transport airframes. It states that aircraft operating around Mach 2 can experience airframe temperatures above 200°F (approximately 93°C), with anticipated service lifetimes exceeding 60,000 hours. The study evaluated candidate Al-Cu-Mg-Ag alloys C415 and C416 and Al-Cu-Li-Mg-Ag alloys RX818 and ML377, comparing them with CM001 and 1143. CM001 was developed for structural use on the Concorde Supersonic Transport; its composition and processing were modified from the British alloy RR58, whose engine-forging applications had demonstrated excellent thermal stability. CM001 processing was tailored to optimize creep resistance while maintaining adequate strength and fracture properties. Thermal exposures were conducted at 200°F, 225°F, and 275°F for up to 30,000 hours, followed by tensile testing from -65°F to 275°F. The candidate alloys had room-temperature yield strengths at least 20% higher than CM001 and 1143 in both as-received and exposed conditions. After 30,000 hours at 200°F and 225°F, C415, C416, and ML377 experienced only minor reductions in strength and elongation, whereas exposure at 275°F caused tensile-strength losses of up to 25% after 15,000 hours. The excerpt does not provide a specific Mach 2.4 HSCT skin temperature or confirm the 100–120°C Concorde value.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The search for innovative solutions in the field of construction materials used in aircraft manufacturing has led to the development of composite materials, particularly CFRP polymer composites. Composite airframe components, which are required to have high strength, are joined using mechanical fasteners. Considering that the composite consists of a polymer matrix, which is a material susceptible to rheological phenomena occurring rapidly at elevated temperature, there is a high probability of significant changes in the strength and performance properties. Coupled thermal and mechanical loads on composite material joints occur in everyday aircraft operation. Experimental tests were conducted using a quasi-isotropic CFRP on an epoxy resin matrix with aerospace certification. The assessment of changes in the strength parameters of the material itself showed a decrease of approx. 40% in its short-term strength at 80 °C compared to the ambient temperature and a decrease in the load-bearing capacity of single-lap bolted joints of over 25%. Even more rapid changes were observed when assessing the fatigue life of the joints assessed at ambient and elevated temperature. In addition, the actual glass transition temperature of the resin was determined using the DSC technique. Analysis of the damage mechanisms showed that at 80 °C, the main degradation mechanisms of the material are accelerated creep processes of the CFRP and softening of the matrix, increasing its susceptibility to damage in the joint area.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This study investigates the impact of temperature variations on the torque capacity of shrink-fit junctions in water-jacketed permanent magnet synchronous motors. Focusing on both baseline and improved designs; torque capacities were evaluated across a temperature range from −40 °C to 120 °C under different material conditions: Least material condition, nominal, and maximum material condition. The baseline design exhibited torque capacities from 7648 Nm to 9032 Nm at −40 °C, decreasing significantly to 549 Nm to 1533 Nm at 120 °C. The improved design showed enhanced performance, with torque capacities ranging from 8055 Nm to 9247 Nm at −40 °C and from 842 Nm to 1618 Nm at 120 °C. The maximum improvement was observed at 120 °C for least material conditions, with a 55.4% increase, and the minimum improvement at −40 °C for maximum material conditions, with a 2.4% increase. Our findings demonstrate a significant increase in torque capacity by up to 20% under varied thermal conditions. These results underscore the effectiveness of design modifications in enhancing thermal stability and torque capacity, making the improved design a more reliable choice for high-performance applications subject to significant thermal fluctuations. This research highlights the critical role of material selection, thermal management, and precise design adjustments in optimizing the performance and reliability of permanent magnet synchronous motors.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'abdallah2018creeplifingmodels pages 16-18'.

Zakaria Abdallah, Karen Perkins, and Cris Arnold. Creep lifing models and techniques. ArXiv, Jan 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.5772/intechopen.71826, doi:10.5772/intechopen.71826. This article has 24 citations.

The excerpt gives useful information on the Wilshire equations and the Monkman–Grant relation, but it does not provide the Larson–Miller parameter equation or a detailed explanation of its operation. The Wilshire method normalizes applied stress by the ultimate tensile strength at the relevant creep temperature, σTS, allowing minimum creep rate, έm, and fracture time, tf, data from different temperatures to be placed on master curves. Its stated relationship combines a normalized-stress power law with an Arrhenius temperature term: έm = M/tf = A*(σ/σTS)^n exp(−Qc*/RT). Here, Qc* is determined from temperature dependence at constant normalized stress, rather than at constant applied stress. The Monkman–Grant relation used in the excerpt is έm = M/tf, linking minimum creep rate to time to fracture and therefore enabling rupture-life estimation from creep-rate measurements. The text cautions that Wilshire extrapolation may still be unreliable because the stress exponent n can fall unpredictably as σ/σTS decreases, although the method can reduce the number of tests needed for long-term strength assessment. It also reports accurate long-term creep-rupture estimates in one cited study, even across changes from transgranular to intergranular fracture. Larson–Miller is mentioned only as a comparison model, without its equation or parameter definition.

## pqac-00000019

From text 'taminger1999analysisofcreep pages 30-34'.

K Taminger. Analysis of creep behavior and parametric models for 2124 al and 2124+ sic composite. Unknown journal, 1999.

The excerpt describes parametric extrapolation methods for predicting creep life and stress-rupture behavior, primarily the Larson–Miller method. Larson–Miller combines absolute temperature and a time measure into a parameter, conventionally written as P_LM = T(C + log10 t), where T is absolute temperature, t is time to rupture or to a specified creep-strain level, and C is an empirical constant. When time is measured in hours, C is commonly approximated as 20, although it may be determined empirically by extrapolating isostress data. A master relationship between P_LM and stress can then be used to estimate allowable stress, rupture time, or time to a specified strain at another temperature. Minimum creep rate may replace time when predicting creep rates rather than lifetimes. The method assumes steady-state, power-law creep and is unsuitable when a major phase change occurs, though it accounts for diffusion-related metallurgical changes. The excerpt also notes that parametric models superimpose data from different test conditions and provide more reliable extrapolation than simple linear steady-state extrapolation. Wilshire equations and the Monkman–Grant relation are not discussed in this excerpt, so their equations and mechanisms cannot be supported from the supplied text.

The excerpt discusses the Wilshire minimum-creep-strain-rate (MCSR) model and the Monkman–Grant relation, but it does not provide the Larson–Miller parameter or its equation. The Wilshire formulation relates the minimum creep strain rate to normalized stress, using the ultimate tensile strength (σTS), in the form εmin = [−ln(σ/σTS)]^(1/k2) (with the excerpt’s notation appearing partly corrupted). Its corresponding stress-rupture/life equation is obtained in the listed rupture-model table and is expressed approximately as tr = [−ln(σ/σTS)]^(−1/k1), with fitted material constants and possible temperature dependence. The model predicts creep behavior by mapping applied stress relative to tensile strength into either the minimum creep rate or rupture time. The Monkman–Grant relation connects minimum creep rate to rupture life through an inverse relationship: tr = kMG/εmin, where tr is time to rupture, εmin is the minimum creep strain rate, and kMG is the Monkman–Grant constant. Thus, a measured or modeled minimum creep rate can be converted into predicted rupture time. The excerpt also states that temperature dependence is represented by an Arrhenius factor, εmin = C exp(−Qc/RT), where Qc is creep activation energy, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature.

## pqac-00000026

From text 'michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 26-28'.

Richard A. Michi, Alex Plotkowski, Amit Shyam, Ryan R. Dehoff, and Sudarsanam Suresh Babu. Towards high-temperature applications of aluminium alloys enabled by additive manufacturing. This article has 389 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports that LPBF aluminum alloys generally lose tensile strength as temperature rises, while elongation increases because of greater dislocation mobility, possible climb, and grain-boundary sliding. Compressive yield strengths can appear much higher than tensile values, although the comparison is affected by defect sensitivity, micropillar size effects, and differing strain rates. AM Al-Si-Mg serves as a baseline and loses strength above approximately 200°C because high-diffusivity Si promotes coarsening of the reinforcing eutectic network, reducing Orowan strengthening. Al-Mg-Sc-Zr and related Al-Mg-Si-Sc-Zr or Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloys benefit from grain refinement by Al3(Zr,Sc), Mg/Mn solid-solution strengthening, and refined intermetallic networks. Other alloys lose strength through coarsening of strengthening precipitates, including Al2Cu and Mg2Si above 200°C. Reinforced alloys can retain high-temperature strength through Orowan looping, load transfer, grain refinement, stable eutectic/intermetallic networks, or high reinforcement fractions. The excerpt provides elevated-temperature tensile and compression data, test temperatures, soak times, strain rates, and orientations, but does not provide dedicated creep-rate, rupture-life, or long-duration creep datasets. It emphasizes that thermal stability can differ substantially: Al-Ce eutectic morphology remains stable, whereas Al-Ce-Mn microstructure evolves with time despite retained strength.

## pqac-00000027

From text 'michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 25-26'.

International Materials Reviews, 67:298-345, Jul 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1080/09506608.2021.1951580, doi:10.1080/09506608.2021.1951580. This article has 389 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt emphasizes that reliable elevated-temperature property data for LPBF aluminum alloys remain sparse: although ambient-temperature properties are commonly reported, “there is little published data” at high temperature. For LPBF Al-Mg-Sc-Zr and related Al-based high-temperature precipitation-strengthened alloys, rapid solidification creates supersaturated solid solutions. Aging can therefore produce larger volume fractions of coarsening-resistant L12 Al3(Sc,Zr)-type nanoprecipitates than in cast alloys (the excerpt contrasts approximately 0.3% with approximately 1–3%), helping retain strength during heating. The principal strength-loss concern is precipitate coarsening or loss of strengthening, although the L12 phase is specifically identified as resistant to coarsening. The excerpt provides no direct creep curve or quantitative creep data for LPBF Al-Mg-Sc-Zr. For LPBF Al-Si-Mg, it cites high-temperature-strength work on material containing 2 vol.% TiCN, but says the ceramic-dispersion coarsening behavior was not reported. Comparable studies involve Al-TiC and TiB2-reinforced alloys. Ceramic dispersions are expected to be thermally stable below roughly 500°C, while reinforcement spheroidization, coarsening, loss of coherency, and weakened interfaces can reduce load-transfer strengthening. A separate Al-Fe-Cr alloy retained strength relatively well after 570°C annealing, attributed to coarsening-resistant phases; this is annealing evidence rather than LPBF creep data.

The excerpt provides elevated-temperature tensile data for LPBF-manufactured Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, but it does not report Al-Si-Mg results, comparative data for other AM aluminum alloys, or creep measurements. The alloy has a bimodal microstructure: columnar grains occur in melt-pool interiors, while equiaxed/fine-grained regions form near melt-pool boundaries. Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitates promote heterogeneous nucleation, refine the grain structure, and help reduce cracking. After a 350 °C, 4 h thermal treatment, room-temperature tensile strength and elongation are 560.6 MPa and 11.1%. Strength decreases markedly as test temperature rises, while ductility generally increases: 435.1 MPa and 25.8% at 100 °C; 269.4 MPa and 20.1% at 150 °C; 102.8 MPa and 47.9% at 200 °C; and 54.0 MPa and 72.2% at 250 °C. These results demonstrate severe high-temperature softening, although the excerpt does not identify the precise mechanisms of strength loss, such as precipitate coarsening/dissolution, recovery, grain-boundary weakening, or enhanced diffusion. It also contains no creep strain, creep-rate, rupture-life, or long-term thermal-stability data.

This excerpt provides elevated-temperature tensile data for LPBF Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, but no creep tests, long-duration thermal-stability measurements, or direct data for Al-Si-Mg or other aluminum alloys. The alloy’s strength decreases sharply as temperature rises, while elongation increases, indicating a pronounced strength–ductility trade-off. Reported tensile strength/elongation pairs are 435.1 MPa/25.8% at 100 °C, 269.4 MPa/20.1% at 150 °C, 102.8 MPa/47.9% at 200 °C, and 54.0 MPa/72.2% at 250 °C. Tensile properties were modestly higher in the build H direction than in the Z direction, with differences below 5%. The microstructure consists of aligned melt pools with a bimodal grain structure: fine equiaxed grains at melt-pool boundaries and larger equiaxed grains in pool interiors; EBSD showed an even dislocation distribution without preferred texture. Fracture surfaces contained many dimples, consistent with ductile fracture. The authors associate these features with Al3(Sc,Zr) second-phase particles: under high external force, dislocations around the particles become active and fracture occurs when particle–matrix interfacial bonding is exceeded. ## pqac-00000041

From text 'singh2025materialvulnerabilitiesin pages 12-14'.

S Singh and K Agarwal. Material vulnerabilities in aviation: a comparative study of hiduminium rr58 in the concorde. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt describes a temperature-related vulnerability of Concorde’s Hiduminium RR58 aluminum fuselage alloy, although it does not explicitly establish that inadequate elevated-temperature property data caused a particular accident or design change. At approximately 127°C, representative of Concorde fuselage operating temperatures, copper- and magnesium-based strengthening precipitates coarsened through Ostwald ripening. Their reduced effectiveness lowered yield strength over time, increasing susceptibility to permanent plastic deformation under operational and repeated mechanical loads, especially around joints and other hot or highly stressed areas. The same microstructural degradation reduced fatigue resistance: coarsened precipitates became less effective at impeding dislocations and crack growth, allowing microcrack initiation and propagation under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses. Fasteners, joints, and constrained regions were identified as likely fatigue-critical locations, with eventual cracking potentially compromising fuselage integrity. The passage also identifies a creep concern: above roughly 120°C, grain-boundary precipitates lose their pinning effectiveness, facilitating grain-boundary sliding and greater creep deformation. Thus, the relevant aerospace anomaly is long-term thermal degradation of RR58 strength, fatigue resistance, and creep resistance during Concorde service, rather than a documented data omission or specific corrective design change.

From text 'taminger1999analysisofcreep pages 13-17'.

K Taminger. Analysis of creep behavior and parametric models for 2124 al and 2124+ sic composite. Unknown journal, 1999.

The excerpt does not identify a specific aerospace accident, failure, or anomaly caused by missing or inadequate elevated-temperature mechanical-property data. It instead explains why elevated-temperature behavior became a major design concern for supersonic aircraft. At Mach 2, aerodynamic heating raises aluminum skin temperatures to approximately 200–225°F, and much of the Concorde’s thermal profile was above 200°F. These temperatures made creep relevant, unlike in typical subsonic aircraft design. The text notes that heating under applied stress can produce thermal expansion, thermal stresses, metallurgical changes, overaging, and long-term creep. It also indicates that aluminum temperatures from 75°F to 250°F can be sufficient to cause overaging and creep over extended periods. As a design response, the Concorde’s RR58/CM.001 alloy—related to 2618—was selected and processed specifically for elevated-temperature creep strength, damage tolerance, and durability. The excerpt mentions the cancellation of the U.S. Supersonic Transport program because it was not economically viable, but it does not attribute that outcome to thermal-property-data deficiencies. Thus, the passage supports a general example of temperature-driven material selection and design change, rather than a documented failure resulting from inadequate data.

From text 'taminger1999analysisofcreep pages 30-34'.

K Taminger. Analysis of creep behavior and parametric models for 2124 al and 2124+ sic composite. Unknown journal, 1999.

The excerpt does not describe a specific aerospace failure, accident, or unexpected high-temperature property loss caused by inadequate data. It does provide an example of an aerospace design and materials-development response to elevated-temperature creep requirements: the Concorde alloy CM.001 was selected and modified through iron additions and thermomechanical processing to create a fine dispersion of Al-Fe intermetallic particles and improve creep resistance. Concorde design used a stringent limit of 0.1% permanent strain over the aircraft lifetime, reflecting the importance of creep data in structural sizing and allowable stresses. Because full-life creep tests were impractical, the text discusses extrapolation methods and their limitations. Simple steady-state extrapolation might fail to account for tertiary creep and cannot reliably predict rupture before the design life. Accelerated testing through higher stress or temperature could also produce misleading results because it may change the active deformation mechanism, making the data less representative of service conditions. Thus, the passage supports an example of alloy and processing changes driven by creep-property requirements, as well as concerns about uncertainty in elevated-temperature data, but it does not document a failure or anomaly resulting from missing or inadequate property information.

The excerpt describes dynamic strain aging (DSA) and Portevin–Le Chatelier (PLC) serrated flow in commercial 5019 aluminum alloy, a 5xxx-series Al-Mg alloy. Across −60 °C to room temperature (RT), ultimate tensile strength and elongation at failure decreased; the reduced ductility was associated with more pronounced DSA and lower strain-rate sensitivity (SRS). PLC occurrence was identified by negative SRS and mapped as a function of temperature and strain rate, but the excerpt does not provide a complete numerical temperature/strain-rate boundary for all aerospace 2xxx, 5xxx, and 7xxx alloys. For F-temper 5019 at −32 °C, changing strain rate from 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³ s⁻¹ slightly reduced the critical strain for serration onset, while at RT increasing the rate from 10⁻³ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹ increased the critical strain. Serrations therefore occur within temperature–strain-rate domains rather than at one universal condition. The measured activation energy for PLC onset in this 5019 alloy was approximately 56 kJ/mol (0.58 eV), higher than the 44–55 kJ/mol reported for onset of A-type serrations in Al-5 wt.% Mg and lower than 83 kJ/mol reported for another Al-Mg alloy. No activation energies or PLC conditions for 2xxx or 7xxx alloys are given in this excerpt.

The front spool stages are limited primarily by low-cycle fatigue (LCF), whereas the final two stages are creep limited, indicating that creep becomes increasingly important at the hotter rear compressor stages. Fan blades and multiple compressor airfoil stages are generally life limited by high-cycle fatigue (HCF), with impact resistance also important. The excerpt does not give numerical creep or fatigue limits for Ti-6Al-4V, Ti-6242, or IMI834, nor does it provide explicit temperature ranges for discs, blisks, and blades. | Application/Location | Typical Temperature Range | Representative Material(s) | Primary Concern |

| Concorde Mach 2 skin | Approximately **100–127°C**; long-life alloy studies used **93, 107, and 135°C** exposures for as long as **30,000 h** | RR58/CM001 (2618-type Al–Cu–Mg alloy) | Immediate strength/modulus reduction plus cumulative overaging, precipitate coarsening, creep, fatigue degradation, and thermally induced stress (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000041) |
| NASA HSCT Mach 2.4 skin | Location- and trajectory-dependent; candidate aluminum structures were evaluated around **93–135°C**, with **93–107°C** emerging as a practical long-duration range | Al–Cu–Mg–Ag and Al–Cu–Li–Mg–Ag candidates; CM001 and 1143 baselines | Retaining strength, creep resistance, fracture properties, and dimensional stability over an intended life exceeding **60,000 h**; no single whole-airframe temperature is defensible (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000016) |
| Hypersonic Mach 5–10 skin and leading edges | Broadly **315°C to >1,480°C**, depending on location and trajectory; large areas may approach **1,370°C**, and a studied forebody reached about **1,140–1,480°C** | Titanium alloys/Ti-matrix composites in cooler zones; nickel superalloys; carbon–carbon and ceramic-matrix composites in hottest zones | Creep, oxidation, thermal shock, acoustic fatigue, severe thermal gradients, loss of stiffness, and the need for insulation or active cooling (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000040) |
| Engine nacelles, pylons, and thrust reversers | **Highly installation-specific**; external structure may be moderately heated, while local hot-air, exhaust, or fire zones can enter regimes where aluminum softens and titanium or heat-resistant alloys are required | Aluminum in cooler structure; titanium, corrosion-resistant steel, and nickel alloys near hot zones | Thermal gradients, joint/preload relaxation, hot-air leakage, oxidation, fatigue, and short-duration fire survivability; component-specific qualification temperatures are required rather than one generic value |
| Bleed-air ducts | **System-specific, commonly several hundred degrees Celsius**; exact design temperature depends on compressor extraction stage and pressure | Titanium, stainless steel, and nickel alloys; insulated flexible joints | Sustained-pressure creep, oxidation, thermal-cycle fatigue, stress relaxation at joints, and consequences of duct rupture; direct system specifications are needed for a defensible numeric limit |
| Compressor stages—front | Generally within conventional titanium capability; titanium alloys have an overall engine-use ceiling near **600°C**, but actual front stages are cooler | Ti‑6Al‑4V in early compressor stages | Low-cycle fatigue of disks and high-cycle fatigue/impact damage of airfoils dominate before creep becomes controlling (pqac-00000063) |
| Compressor stages—rear, including wheels and impellers | Approaches the upper titanium range, approximately **500–600°C** in the hottest titanium applications; hotter stages require nickel alloys | Creep-resistant Ti‑6242S or IMI834; nickel-base alloys beyond titanium capability | Creep and creep-fatigue become controlling; rear stages can be creep-limited even where front stages remain fatigue-limited (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000068) |
| Turbine blades, combustors, and hot-section heat exchangers | Superalloy structures commonly serve around **760–1,093°C**; representative TMF tests span **500–1,000°C**, and combustor service can approach **1,000°C** | Directionally solidified or single-crystal nickel superalloys; Haynes 230; coated systems | Creep rupture, oxidation/hot corrosion, TMF, dwell-sensitive creep-fatigue, coating degradation, and crack growth under combined thermal and mechanical cycling (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000062) |
| Rocket or scramjet nozzle skin, uncooled | Can exceed **1,650°C**; one analysis predicted about **2.0–2.83 MW/m²** heat flux | Actively cooled titanium/Ti-matrix face sheets in studied concepts; refractory, carbon–carbon, or ceramic systems elsewhere | Passive structures may be untenable: rapid strength loss, creep, oxidation, thermal fatigue, and burn-through drive regenerative or active cooling (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000034) |
