**Heating methods and temperature control.** Elevated-temperature tensile testing (ASTM E21) typically employs resistance (split-tube) furnaces, with temperature maintained within ±5 °F (±2.8 °C) across the gauge section, as demonstrated in a comprehensive evaluation of elevated-temperature tensile practice (manning1960anevaluationof pages 9-14). Temperature is monitored by multiple thermocouples attached directly to the specimen gauge section (lee2013experimentalinvestigationof pages 1-2, lee2013experimentalinvestigationof pages 4-5). Induction heating and radiant-lamp furnaces are also used, particularly for TMF where rapid heating rates (e.g., 6.94 °C/s) are required (shi2026experimentalandintrinsic pages 7-10).

**Strain-rate control.** Historical ASTM E21 practice specified strain rates of approximately 0.005 min⁻¹ up to yield and 0.05 min⁻¹ thereafter, emphasizing that rates must be measured in the specimen gauge length rather than from crosshead speed (manning1960anevaluationof pages 9-14). Elevated-temperature tensile testing of steel at rates of 0.01 and 0.1 in./min showed that loading rate strongly affects measured strength above 600 °C, underscoring the need for rate control (lee2013experimentalinvestigationof pages 1-2).

**High-temperature extensometry.** Air-cooled high-temperature extensometers (e.g., MTS 632.54E-11 with 1-inch gauge length and −5% to +10% strain range) are used for elevated-temperature tensile tests; resetting is required when large strains are anticipated (lee2013experimentalinvestigationof pages 1-2, lee2013experimentalinvestigationof pages 4-5). For TMF, axial extensometers must simultaneously track mechanical strain while the temperature gradient across the gauge section is maintained within 15 °C (shi2026experimentalandintrinsic pages 7-10).

**Soak time.** Temperature stabilization prior to loading is critical. Reported practice reached target temperature in approximately 20 minutes followed by a one-hour soak (lee2013experimentalinvestigationof pages 4-5). For creep testing (ASTM E139), thermal equilibrium must be established before load application; test durations may extend to 25,000 hours (messner2023asmecodequalification pages 65-68).

**Creep and stress-rupture testing (ASTM E139/ISO 204)** records minimum creep rate, time to specified strain (e.g., 0.1%, 0.2%, 1.0%), onset of tertiary creep, and rupture time under constant load at constant temperature. For AM qualification, one proposed plan specified testing from 500 to 900 °C with six replicates per condition (messner2023asmecodequalification pages 65-68).

**TMF testing (ASTM E2368)** independently and simultaneously cycles temperature and mechanical strain fields. Representative Ni-superalloy tests used 500–1,000 °C temperature ranges, 0.5–1.0% mechanical strain amplitudes, 72-second heating/cooling ramps, and optional 60- or 300-second peak-temperature holds (shi2026experimentalandintrinsic pages 7-10, shi2026experimentalandintrinsic pages 4-7).

**Creep–fatigue testing (ASTM E2714)** uses strain- or force-controlled cycling with extended elevated-temperature hold periods. It evaluates whether dwell-enhanced damage reduces life below predictions from separate fatigue and creep data. Hold times of 1,200 seconds have been employed in superalloy studies (slotwinski2012mechanicalpropertiestesting pages 9-12, moverare2025areviewof pages 5-6).

## 5. Failures, Anomalies, and Design Changes Traced to Elevated-Temperature Property Considerations

**Concorde RR58 thermal degradation.** The Concorde's Hiduminium RR58 (2618A) alloy experienced cumulative thermal degradation at skin temperatures of approximately 120–127 °C over thousands of flight cycles. Cu- and Mg-based strengthening precipitates coarsened through Ostwald ripening, reducing yield strength and fatigue resistance over time. Above approximately 120 °C, grain-boundary precipitates lost their pinning effectiveness, facilitating grain-boundary sliding and increased creep deformation. Joints, fastener holes, and constrained regions were identified as fatigue-critical locations where thermally degraded properties could compromise structural integrity (singh2025materialvulnerabilitiesin pages 12-14). This experience directly motivated the development and testing of improved Al–Cu–Mg–Ag alloys with 20%+ higher yield strength than CM001 for the HSCT program (jr2004effectofthermal pages 1-5, jr2004effectofthermal pages 25-28). **[Strongly supported by multiple sources.]**

**Alloy selection driven by creep data.** The Concorde's selection of RR58/CM001 over other aluminum alloys was explicitly driven by elevated-temperature creep data: the alloy was processed with iron additions and thermomechanical treatment to create Al–Fe intermetallic dispersoids that improved creep resistance, and a 0.1% permanent-strain lifetime limit was enforced (taminger1999analysisofcreep pages 30-34). This represents a design change relative to conventional subsonic-aircraft practice, where creep is negligible. The subsequent HSCT program's replacement of CM001 with candidate alloys C415, C416, and ML377—which maintained stability up to 30,000 hours at 200–225 °F—was similarly driven by improved thermal-exposure data (jr2004effectofthermal pages 25-28). **[Strongly supported.]**

**Compressor-stage alloy selection.** The transition from Ti-6Al-4V in front compressor stages to Ti-6242S in rear stages, and ultimately to nickel-base superalloys in the hottest stages, is directly driven by creep data: front stages are fatigue-limited, while rear stages are creep-limited (williams2003progressinstructural pages 17-19). An alloy selected on the basis of room-temperature fatigue and tensile data alone would be inadequate for the rear compressor stages. The selection of 2124 aluminum for certain applications was later revised to other alloys with improved fatigue strength, illustrating the consequences of incomplete property characterization (williams2003progressinstructural pages 17-19). **[Strongly supported.]**

**Insufficient high-temperature data for LPBF alloys.** A comprehensive review concluded that evaluations of high-temperature mechanical properties and corrosion responses of additively manufactured aluminum alloys are "severely deficient," with little published data above 200 °C and essentially no creep or stress-rupture data for most LPBF aluminum systems (michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 25-26). This deficiency directly limits the qualification of LPBF aluminum alloys for any elevated-temperature aerospace application. **[Strongly supported.]**

## 6. Implications for LPBF Aluminum Alloy Development

The BYU Vertical Cloud Lab's current test ladder—single tracks, density cubes, and room-temperature tensile bars—captures printability and baseline mechanical properties but cannot evaluate any of the temperature-dependent, time-dependent, or rate-dependent phenomena described above. The following data quantify the gap:

| Alloy System | Condition/Heat Treatment | Test Temperature (°C) | UTS (MPa) | Elongation (%) | Reference |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|

| LPBF AlSi10Mg | Stress-relieved at 350°C for 2 h | 125 | Not reported in available excerpt | Not reported in available excerpt | (lehmhus2022hightemperaturemechanicalproperties pages 1-2) |
| LPBF AlSi10Mg | Stress-relieved at 350°C for 2 h | 250 | 162.8 | 15.6 | (lehmhus2022hightemperaturemechanicalproperties pages 1-2) |
| LPBF AlSi10Mg | Stress-relieved at 350°C for 2 h | 450 | 34.4 | 26.5 | (lehmhus2022hightemperaturemechanicalproperties pages 1-2) |

| LPBF Al–Mg–Sc–Zr | Thermally treated at 350°C for 4 h | 100 | 435.1 | 25.8 | (ren2024studyonmicrostructure pages 1-2, ren2024studyonmicrostructure pages 13-14) |
| LPBF Al–Mg–Sc–Zr | Thermally treated at 350°C for 4 h | 150 | 269.4 | 20.1 | (ren2024studyonmicrostructure pages 1-2, ren2024studyonmicrostructure pages 13-14) |

*Table: Elevated-temperature tensile results show severe thermal softening and generally increased ductility in two LPBF aluminum systems. Values unavailable in the retrieved source excerpt are explicitly identified rather than inferred.*

For LPBF AlSi10Mg, the eutectic silicon network that provides strengthening at room temperature coarsens and spheroidizes above approximately 200 °C, destroying Orowan strengthening (michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 26-28, wang2024areviewon pages 7-9). For LPBF Al–Mg–Sc–Zr alloys—closer to the BYU lab's design space of critical-mineral-lean compositions with Sc, Zr, and potentially Ce—L1₂ Al₃(Sc,Zr) nanoprecipitates provide better coarsening resistance, but rapid solidification produces supersaturated solid solutions that evolve upon thermal exposure, and the volume fraction and stability of these precipitates directly control elevated-temperature strength retention (michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 26-28, michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 25-26).

**Recommended elevated-temperature tests to add**, in approximate priority order based on the evidence reviewed:

1. **Elevated-temperature tensile testing (ASTM E21/ISO 6892-2)** at 100–300 °C, to quantify instantaneous strength retention.
2. **Thermal-exposure testing followed by room-temperature tensile testing**, at 150–300 °C for 100–10,000 hours, to assess overaging and precipitate coarsening.
3. **Creep and stress-rupture testing (ASTM E139/ISO 204)** at 150–300 °C under representative stresses, to determine whether LPBF microstructures resist time-dependent deformation.
4. **Stress-relaxation testing (ASTM E328)** if fastener or interference-fit applications are anticipated.
5. **Low-cycle fatigue at temperature (ASTM E606)** and potentially creep–fatigue testing (ASTM E2714), if cyclic thermal-mechanical loading is expected.
6. **Fatigue-crack growth at temperature** and thermal-cycle testing, to evaluate damage tolerance in the presence of LPBF defects at elevated temperature.

These tests will close the "severely deficient" data gap identified for LPBF aluminum alloys (michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 25-26) and position the alloys for aerospace qualification in thermal environments where room-temperature data alone provide no assurance of structural integrity.

A representative practice maintained temperature within **±5 °F (±2.8 °C)**; historical E21 practice used strain rates near **0.005 min⁻¹ to yield** and approximately **0.05 min⁻¹ thereafter**. Temperature should be measured at multiple gauge-section locations after stabilization; use a calibrated high-temperature extensometer rather than crosshead displacement. Exact limits depend on the adopted edition. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046) | Measures yield strength, UTS, elongation, and stress–strain response **while hot**—properties that room-temperature testing after cooling cannot supply. |
| **ISO 6892-2** | Metallic materials—tensile testing—Part 2: method of test at elevated temperature | International counterpart to elevated-temperature tensile practice. Requires controlled heating, temperature measurement and stabilization over the parallel length, specified strain-rate control, and suitable extensometry. Laboratories must follow the limits and rate method in the current edition rather than importing ASTM E21 values without verification. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046) | Supports internationally comparable hot-tension data and qualification of alloys, product forms, and additively manufactured material. |
| **ASTM E139** | Creep, creep-rupture, and stress-rupture tests of metallic materials | Applies sustained load or stress at controlled temperature and records creep strain versus time, minimum creep rate, time to specified strain, onset of tertiary creep, rupture time, and rupture elongation. Long programs can extend to thousands or tens of thousands of hours; one LPBF qualification plan proposed **500–900 °C** tests lasting up to **25,000 h**. (pqac-00000009) | Provides deformation and life data for continuously loaded hot structures, rotating engine parts, ducts, fasteners, and pressure-containing components—behavior absent from short tensile tests. |
| **ISO 204** | Metallic materials—uniaxial creep testing in tension | International creep-test method covering constant-temperature, sustained-force or sustained-stress testing; temperature stability, alignment, load accuracy, strain measurement, rupture time, and post-test elongation must be controlled and reported. | Enables internationally consistent creep and rupture datasets for long-duration design and time–temperature extrapolation. |
| **ASTM E328** | Stress-relaxation testing of materials and structures | Holds total strain or displacement approximately constant at controlled temperature and measures the decline in stress with time. The test definition specifies initial strain or stress, loading history, temperature, duration, and relaxation-measurement method. | Quantifies loss of bolt preload, seal or gasket compression, interference-fit force, and residual constraint during hot service. |
| **ASTM E606/E606M** | Strain-controlled fatigue testing | Uses cyclic axial-strain control, normally with a calibrated axial extensometer; specifies strain amplitude or range, strain ratio, waveform, frequency or strain rate, temperature, environment, and failure criterion. Dedicated creep–fatigue characterization with substantial holds belongs under E2714. | Generates low-cycle-fatigue life, stabilized hysteresis loops, cyclic hardening or softening, and Coffin–Manson-type data for starts, stops, and severe thermal transients. |
| **ASTM E2368** | Strain-controlled thermomechanical-fatigue testing | Independently and simultaneously cycles uniform temperature and mechanical-strain fields. Both must be measured and phase-controlled. Representative superalloy tests used **500–1000 °C**, **0.5–1.0% mechanical-strain amplitude**, **72 s** heating and cooling ramps, and optional **60 or 300 s** peak-temperature holds; axial temperature variation was held within **15 °C**. (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058) | Reproduces coupled thermal and mechanical cycling. In-phase loading places maximum tensile strain near maximum temperature; out-of-phase loading places it near minimum temperature, producing different creep, oxidation, and mean-stress damage. (pqac-00000057, pqac-00000061) |
| **ASTM E2714** | Creep–fatigue testing | Uses constant-amplitude strain- or force-controlled cycling with sequential or simultaneous loading that promotes both cyclic and creep damage. It records deformation and crack initiation or nucleation; elevated-temperature dwell periods are substantially longer than in conventional fatigue tests. Service-like studies have used **1200 s** peak-temperature holds. (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059) | Determines whether high-temperature dwell damage reduces life beyond predictions from separate fatigue and creep tests—critical for combustors, hot ducts, engine hardware, and reusable launch structures. |
| **ASTM E1457** | Measurement of creep-crack-growth times and rates in metals | Uses a precracked fracture-mechanics specimen under sustained or slowly varying load at elevated temperature. It tracks crack extension with time and relates growth rate to an appropriate time-dependent crack-tip parameter; temperature, loading history, crack measurement, specimen validity, and transition from fatigue or elastic-plastic behavior require control. | Supplies defect-tolerance and inspection-life data when a pre-existing flaw grows by time-dependent creep, which smooth-bar tensile, creep-rupture, and low-cycle-fatigue tests cannot directly predict. |


*Table: Comparison of the principal ASTM and ISO methods for hot tensile, creep, relaxation, fatigue, thermomechanical-fatigue, creep–fatigue, and creep-crack-growth testing. The table highlights the controlled variables and the aerospace behavior each method reveals.*

| Hypersonic Mach 5–10 skin and leading edges | Broadly **315°C to >1,480°C**, depending on location and trajectory; large areas may approach **1,370°C**, and a studied forebody reached about **1,140–1,480°C** | Titanium alloys/Ti-matrix composites in cooler zones; nickel superalloys; carbon–carbon and ceramic-matrix composites in hottest zones | Creep, oxidation, thermal shock, acoustic fatigue, severe thermal gradients, loss of stiffness, and the need for insulation or active cooling (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000040) |
| Engine nacelles, pylons, and thrust reversers | **Highly installation-specific**; external structure may be moderately heated, while local hot-air, exhaust, or fire zones can enter regimes where aluminum softens and titanium or heat-resistant alloys are required | Aluminum in cooler structure; titanium, corrosion-resistant steel, and nickel alloys near hot zones | Thermal gradients, joint/preload relaxation, hot-air leakage, oxidation, fatigue, and short-duration fire survivability; component-specific qualification temperatures are required rather than one generic value |
| Bleed-air ducts | **System-specific, commonly several hundred degrees Celsius**; exact design temperature depends on compressor extraction stage and pressure | Titanium, stainless steel, and nickel alloys; insulated flexible joints | Sustained-pressure creep, oxidation, thermal-cycle fatigue, stress relaxation at joints, and consequences of duct rupture; direct system specifications are needed for a defensible numeric limit |
| Compressor stages—front | Generally within conventional titanium capability; titanium alloys have an overall engine-use ceiling near **600°C**, but actual front stages are cooler | Ti‑6Al‑4V in early compressor stages | Low-cycle fatigue of disks and high-cycle fatigue/impact damage of airfoils dominate before creep becomes controlling (pqac-00000063) |
| Compressor stages—rear, including wheels and impellers | Approaches the upper titanium range, approximately **500–600°C** in the hottest titanium applications; hotter stages require nickel alloys | Creep-resistant Ti‑6242S or IMI834; nickel-base alloys beyond titanium capability | Creep and creep-fatigue become controlling; rear stages can be creep-limited even where front stages remain fatigue-limited (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000068) |
| Turbine blades, combustors, and hot-section heat exchangers | Superalloy structures commonly serve around **760–1,093°C**; representative TMF tests span **500–1,000°C**, and combustor service can approach **1,000°C** | Directionally solidified or single-crystal nickel superalloys; Haynes 230; coated systems | Creep rupture, oxidation/hot corrosion, TMF, dwell-sensitive creep-fatigue, coating degradation, and crack growth under combined thermal and mechanical cycling (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000062) |
| Rocket or scramjet nozzle skin, uncooled | Can exceed **1,650°C**; one analysis predicted about **2.0–2.83 MW/m²** heat flux | Actively cooled titanium/Ti-matrix face sheets in studied concepts; refractory, carbon–carbon, or ceramic systems elsewhere | Passive structures may be untenable: rapid strength loss, creep, oxidation, thermal fatigue, and burn-through drive regenerative or active cooling (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000034) |
| Structures near rocket engines and TPS substructure | Hot exterior may exceed **1,370°C**, while insulation must hold aluminum or other primary substructure below its allowable temperature; conventional 2219 Al was cited with an upper working temperature near **175°C** | Aluminum primary structure beneath ceramic TPS; titanium, nickel alloys, carbon–carbon, and ceramic insulation in hotter regions | Through-thickness thermal gradients, attachment loads, local TPS damage, heat soak after peak heating, creep/softening of hidden substructure, and differential thermal expansion (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040) |
| Fire exposure | Transient, nonuniform, and scenario-specific; temperatures can rise far above normal-service allowables, so time–temperature–load history governs failure | Aluminum, titanium, steels, nickel alloys, joints, and protected structural assemblies | Rapid modulus and strength loss, thermally accelerated creep, buckling, joint/preload loss, oxidation, and residual-property loss after the fire; fire qualification must use prescribed heat-flux/time histories rather than a single material temperature |

info.query: Why is elevated-temperature mechanical testing important for aerospace structural alloys, and what does it reveal that room-temperature testing does not? Cover, with citations and DOIs: (1) Where aerospace structures get hot: aerodynamic heating of supersonic and hypersonic skins (Concorde at Mach 2 cruise, the NASA High-Speed Research / HSCT program, missiles and hypersonic vehicles), engine nacelles, pylons, thrust reversers and bleed-air ducts, auxiliary power units, compressor wheels and impellers, heat exchangers, structures near rocket engines and thermal-protection-system substructure, and fire exposure. (2) What changes with temperature and with time at temperature: loss of yield and tensile strength, elongation and modulus at temperature; property loss after thermal exposure (overaging, precipitate coarsening) measured back at room temperature; creep, stress rupture and stress relaxation; low-cycle and thermomechanical fatigue and creep-fatigue interaction; fatigue-crack growth and fracture toughness at temperature; oxidation; dynamic strain aging; and how long-time behavior is extrapolated (Larson-Miller, Wilshire, Monkman-Grant). (3) How design allowables handle temperature: MMPDS 'effect of temperature' and 'effect of exposure time' curves (for example 0.5 h to 10,000 h), and how this differs for aluminum, titanium, steels and nickel superalloys. (4) Test standards and practice: ASTM E21 (elevated-temperature tension), ISO 6892-2, ASTM E139 and ISO 204 (creep and stress rupture), ASTM E328 (stress relaxation), ASTM E606 (strain-controlled fatigue), ASTM E2368 (thermomechanical fatigue), ASTM E2714 (creep-fatigue), ASTM E1457 (creep-crack growth); heating methods, temperature-uniformity and soak-time requirements, and high-temperature extensometry. (5) Failures, anomalies or design changes traced to missing or inadequate elevated-temperature property data. Context: the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab designs aluminum alloys for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with AI and CALPHAD, including critical-mineral-lean compositions (less Sc, Li, Ce), makes its own powder by ultrasonic atomization, and tests in a ladder of single tracks, density cubes and room-temperature tensile bars. It is deciding which elevated-temperature, non-tensile and rate-dependent mechanical tests to add. Prefer primary sources, NASA, NIST and AFRL technical reports, MMPDS and standards; give DOIs or report numbers; give numbers with temperatures, exposure times, strain rates and units; and say which claims are strongly vs. weakly supported.
